claim: Average cable length in wild-type haploid cells is 4.5 ± 0.3 µm.
source: Average cable length and average cell length were remarkably similar (4.5 ± 0.3 µm and 4.5 ± 0.2 µm, respectively), suggesting a scaling relationship.
evidence: Directly stated measurement from experimental data on cable lengths in fixed cells.

claim: Average cell length in wild-type haploid cells is 4.5 ± 0.2 µm.
source: Average cable length and average cell length were remarkably similar (4.5 ± 0.3 µm and 4.5 ± 0.2 µm, respectively), suggesting a scaling relationship.
evidence: Directly stated measurement from experimental data on cell lengths in fixed cells.

claim: Cable lengths range from 2.0–8.7 µm in wild-type haploid cells.
source: However, we note that there was a wider range in cable lengths (2.0–8.7 µm) compared to cell lengths (3.7–5.5 µm), presumably because cables in fixed cells are at different stages of growth.
evidence: Directly stated measurement range from experimental data.

claim: Cell lengths range from 3.7–5.5 µm in wild-type haploid cells.
source: However, we note that there was a wider range in cable lengths (2.0–8.7 µm) compared to cell lengths (3.7–5.5 µm), presumably because cables in fixed cells are at different stages of growth.
evidence: Directly stated measurement range from experimental data.

claim: Cables in fixed cells are at different stages of growth, which explains the wider range in cable lengths compared to cell lengths.
source: However, we note that there was a wider range in cable lengths (2.0–8.7 µm) compared to cell lengths (3.7–5.5 µm), presumably because cables in fixed cells are at different stages of growth.
evidence: Authors provide an interpretation of their data based on the observation of different cable length ranges.

claim: Cables that grow along the cortex of an ellipsoid shaped cell can exceed the length of the cell while not growing past the back of the cell.
source: Further, because cables grow along the cortex of an ellipsoid shaped cell, their length can exceed the length of the cell while not growing past the back of the cell.
evidence: Logical inference based on the geometry of cable growth along a curved surface.

claim: A cable that grows from the bud neck to the back of the cell is expected to be slightly longer than the direct distance between these two points.
source: Therefore, a cable that grows from the bud neck to the back of the cell is expected to be slightly longer than the direct distance between these two points.
evidence: Logical inference based on the geometry of cable growth along a curved surface.

claim: Diploid mother cells have an ~2-fold increase in volume compared to haploid mother cells (81.8 ± 6.3 µm³ versus 44.9 ± 4.7 µm³).
source: Diploid mother cells had an ~2-fold increase in volume compared to haploid mother cells (81.8 ± 6.3 µm3 and 44.9 ± 4.7 µm3, respectively) (Figure 1A,B and E), consistent with previous studies (Jorgensen et al., 2002).
evidence: Directly stated measurement from experimental data, supported by reference to Figure 1E and citation to previous work.

claim: The cdc28-13ts strain exhibits a ~5-fold increase in volume (198.3 ± 5.5 µm³ versus 40.9 ± 2.3 µm³) after growth at the restrictive temperature for 8 hr followed by 1 hr at the permissive temperature.
source: However, this strain displayed a ~ 5-fold increase in volume (198.3 ± 5.5 µm3 versus 40.9 ± 2.3 µm3) after growth at the restrictive temperature (37°C) for 8 hr, followed by 1 hr of growth at the permissive temperature (25°C) to allow cell polarization and bud growth (Figure 1C,D and E; and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C; Allard et al., 2018).
evidence: Directly stated measurement from experimental data, supported by reference to figures and citation.

claim: Cell length increases with cell volume.
source: Accordingly, cell length increased with cell volume (Figure 1F).
evidence: Stated relationship supported by reference to Figure 1F showing the data.

claim: Cable length is greater in diploids (6.3 ± 0.7 µm) compared to haploids (4.5 ± 0.3 µm).
source: Cable length was greater in diploids (6.3 ± 0.7 µm) compared to haploids (4.5 ± 0.3 µm), and greater in induced (8.2 ± 0.4 µm) compared to uninduced (4.3 ± 0.1 µm) cdc28-13ts cells (Figure 1G).
evidence: Directly stated measurement from experimental data, supported by reference to Figure 1G.

claim: Cable length is greater in induced cdc28-13ts cells (8.2 ± 0.4 µm) compared to uninduced cdc28-13ts cells (4.3 ± 0.1 µm).
source: Cable length was greater in diploids (6.3 ± 0.7 µm) compared to haploids (4.5 ± 0.3 µm), and greater in induced (8.2 ± 0.4 µm) compared to uninduced (4.3 ± 0.1 µm) cdc28-13ts cells (Figure 1G).
evidence: Directly stated measurement from experimental data, supported by reference to Figure 1G.

claim: The distribution of cable lengths for all strains collapses when cable lengths are divided by the lengths of the cells in which they grew.
source: However, the distribution of cable lengths for all strains collapsed when we divided the lengths of cables by the lengths of the cells in which they grew (Figure 1H and I).
evidence: Directly stated observation from data analysis, supported by reference to Figures 1H and I.

claim: Cables grow to a length that matches cell length.
source: These results strongly suggest that cables grow to a length that matches cell length.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the collapsed distribution of cable length/cell length ratios.

claim: The ratio of cable length to cell length and the scaling exponents are similar for cells of different morphologies (different aspect ratios).
source: Despite these differences in cell shape, the ratio of cable length to cell length, and the scaling exponents were similar for all cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C–G).
evidence: Stated observation from analysis of cells with different aspect ratios, supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 2C–G.

claim: In cells of vastly different size and shape, cable length directly scales with cell length rather than with cell surface area or volume.
source: Therefore, in cells of vastly different size and shape, the cable length directly scales with cell length, rather than with other dimensions such as cell surface area or volume.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the analysis of cells with different aspect ratios showing consistent scaling with length.

claim: Initially, cables extend at 0.36 ± 0.02 µm s⁻¹.
source: Initially cables extended at 0.36 ± 0.02 µm s−1, and as they grew longer their extension rates steadily decreased (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Directly stated measurement from live imaging experiments, supported by Figure 2F.

claim: As cables grow longer, their extension rates steadily decrease.
source: Initially cables extended at 0.36 ± 0.02 µm s−1, and as they grew longer their extension rates steadily decreased (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Directly stated observation from live imaging experiments, supported by Figure 2F.

claim: Greater changes in cable length occur during earlier phases of cable growth.
source: Accordingly, we observed greater changes in cable length during earlier phases of cable growth (Figure 2G, Figure 2—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: Directly stated observation from live imaging experiments, supported by Figure 2G.

claim: Cables decelerate as they lengthen.
source: Thus, as cables lengthen their growth rate decelerates.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the observation that extension rates decrease as cables grow longer.

claim: Very short cables (<2 µm) detected by live imaging were not seen in analysis of fixed cells.
source: Note that we detected cables that were very short (<2 µm) by live imaging, which were not seen in our analysis of fixed cells.
evidence: Directly stated observation comparing live imaging and fixed cell data.

claim: Shorter cables extend at a faster rate compared to longer cables and are therefore less prevalent in fixed cell populations.
source: We expect that this is because shorter cables extend at a faster rate compared to longer cables and are therefore less prevalent in fixed cell populations.
evidence: Explanation provided by authors for why short cables are not seen in fixed cells.

claim: Cables are longer in smy1∆ compared to wildtype cells.
source: We confirmed the increase in cable length in smy1∆ cells (Figure 3A, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B; Eskin et al., 2016), but found that cables continued to decelerate in the absence of Smy1 (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: Stated observation from experimental data, supported by Figure 3A and citation to previous work.

claim: Cables continue to decelerate in the absence of Smy1.
source: We confirmed the increase in cable length in smy1∆ cells (Figure 3A, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B; Eskin et al., 2016), but found that cables continued to decelerate in the absence of Smy1 (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: Directly stated observation from live imaging experiments, supported by Figures 3B and C.

claim: The initial cable extension rate in smy1Δ cells (0.42 ± 0.04 µm s⁻¹) is increased compared to wild-type cells (0.35 ± 0.02 µm s⁻¹).
source: Furthermore, we observed an increase in the initial cable extension rate in smy1Δ (0.42 ± 0.04 µm s−1) compared to wild-type cells (0.35 ± 0.02 µm s−1) (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: Directly stated measurement from live imaging experiments, supported by Figures 3D and E.

claim: The initial extension rate in smy1Δ cells increases by 1.2-fold ± 0.2.
source: Interestingly, the initial extension rate in smy1Δ cells increased by the same magnitude (1.2-fold ± 0.2) as the measured increase in cable length (1.2-fold ± 0.1).
evidence: Directly stated calculation from experimental data.

claim: The measured increase in cable length in smy1Δ cells is 1.2-fold ± 0.1.
source: Interestingly, the initial extension rate in smy1Δ cells increased by the same magnitude (1.2-fold ± 0.2) as the measured increase in cable length (1.2-fold ± 0.1).
evidence: Directly stated calculation from experimental data.

claim: Smy1 affects cable length by limiting the initial cable growth rate but does not provide the feedback that results in cable deceleration.
source: Thus, Smy1 affects cable length by limiting the initial cable growth rate (Figure 3F) but does not provide the feedback that results in cable deceleration.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the observation that cables still decelerate in smy1Δ cells despite increased initial extension rate.

claim: The 1.2-fold increase in initial extension rate in smy1∆ cells leads to a 1.2-fold increase in initial deceleration of cables.
source: Thus, the measured 1.2-fold increase in initial extension rate seen in smy1∆ cells is expected to lead to a 1.2-fold increase in initial deceleration of cables, shortly after they emerge from the bud neck.
evidence: Prediction from the balance-point model that is then tested with experimental data.

claim: Cables begin to grow at similar rates in shorter and longer cdc28-13ts cells.
source: When cables began to grow, they extended at similar rates in shorter and longer cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Directly stated observation from live imaging experiments, supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: As cables grow longer, they decelerate more gradually in longer cells compared to shorter cells.
source: However, as the cables grew longer, they decelerated more gradually in the longer cells (Figure 4D–F).
evidence: Directly stated observation from live imaging experiments, supported by Figures 4D–F.

claim: Cables are longer in longer cells.
source: This led to longer cables in longer cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Directly stated observation from live imaging experiments, supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Once cable length is normalized to cell length, cables extend with similar dynamics in cells of different lengths.
source: Further, once cable length was normalized to cell length, cables extended with similar dynamics (Figure 4G), as predicted by our model.
evidence: Directly stated observation from data analysis, supported by Figure 4G.

claim: Cables grow until their length matches the length of the cell.
source: Collectively, our observations demonstrate that cables grow until their length matches the length of the cell, and that this is achieved by length-dependent deceleration of cable extension.
evidence: Summary conclusion drawn from multiple experimental observations.

claim: Cable length matching is achieved by length-dependent deceleration of cable extension.
source: Collectively, our observations demonstrate that cables grow until their length matches the length of the cell, and that this is achieved by length-dependent deceleration of cable extension.
evidence: Summary conclusion drawn from multiple experimental observations.

claim: Polarized actin cables in S. cerevisiae are linear bundles of crosslinked actin filaments assembled by formins.
source: These cables are linear bundles of crosslinked actin filaments assembled by formins, which extend along the cell cortex and serve as tracks for intracellular transport of cargo from the mother cell to the growing bud, or daughter cell.
evidence: Established knowledge about actin cable structure and function in yeast.

claim: Actin cables extend along the cell cortex and serve as tracks for intracellular transport of cargo from the mother cell to the growing bud.
source: These cables are linear bundles of crosslinked actin filaments assembled by formins, which extend along the cell cortex and serve as tracks for intracellular transport of cargo from the mother cell to the growing bud, or daughter cell.
evidence: Established knowledge about actin cable function in yeast.

claim: Complementary sets of cables are assembled by two formins, Bni1 at the bud tip and Bnr1 at the bud neck.
source: Complementary sets of cables are assembled by two formins, Bni1 at the bud tip and Bnr1 at the bud neck (Pruyne et al., 2004).
evidence: Established knowledge about formin localization and cable assembly, supported by citation.

claim: Throughout the cell cycle, cables are continuously polymerized, turn over at high rates, and appear to grow until they reach the back of the mother cell.
source: Throughout the cell cycle, cables are continuously polymerized, turn over at high rates, and appear to grow until they reach the back of the mother cell (Yu et al., 2011; Yang and Pon, 2002; Eskin et al., 2016).
evidence: Established knowledge about cable dynamics, supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Smy1 directly inhibits Bnr1-mediated actin assembly.
source: It has been reported that cables are longer in smy1∆ compared to wildtype cells, and that Smy1 directly inhibits Bnr1-mediated actin assembly (Eskin et al., 2016; Chesarone-Cataldo et al., 2011).
evidence: Established knowledge from previous studies, supported by citations.

claim: Smy1 is transported by myosin along cables to the bud neck where Bnr1 is anchored.
source: Further, Smy1 is transported by myosin along cables to the bud neck where Bnr1 is anchored.
evidence: Established knowledge about Smy1 transport mechanism.

claim: An 'antenna mechanism' has been proposed in which longer cables deliver more Smy1 to slow cable extension and limit cable length.
source: Based on these observations, an 'antenna mechanism' has been proposed in which longer cables deliver more Smy1 to slow cable extension and limit cable length (Mohapatra et al., 2015).
evidence: Reference to a previously proposed model, supported by citation.

claim: The size of a cell's internal parts are scaled to its overall size.
source: The size of a cell's internal parts are scaled to its overall size. This size-scaling behavior has been demonstrated for organelles as well as large macromolecular assemblies, illustrating the broad importance of adapting the size of internal structures to the geometric dimensions of the cell (Rafelski et al., 2012; Levy and Heald, 2010; Hazel et al., 2013; Good et al., 2013; Weber and Brangwynne, 2015; Greenan et al., 2010; Jorgensen et al., 2007; Decker et al., 2011; Neumann and Nurse, 2007; Lacroix et al., 2018).
evidence: General principle supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: A limiting pool mechanism maintains a constant concentration of molecular components, enabling subcellular structures to increase in size proportionally with cell volume.
source: A popular model of cellular scaling is the limiting pool mechanism, wherein maintaining a constant concentration of molecular components enables the subcellular structure to increase in size proportionally with cell volume (Goehring and Hyman, 2012; de Godoy et al., 2008)
evidence: Description of an established model, supported by citations.

claim: Cells use a limiting pool mechanism to scale the size of their nucleoli, centrosomes, and mitotic spindles.
source: Indeed, cells appear to use a limiting pool mechanism to scale the size of their nucleoli, centrosomes, and mitotic spindles (Hazel et al., 2013; Good et al., 2013; Weber and Brangwynne, 2015; Greenan et al., 2010; Decker et al., 2011; Lacroix et al., 2018).
evidence: Established knowledge about scaling mechanisms for specific organelles, supported by citations.

claim: Limiting pool models cannot explain how the size of a linear subcellular structure scales with the linear dimensions of a cell rather than its volume.
source: However, limiting pool models cannot explain how the size of a linear subcellular structure scales with the linear dimensions of a cell, rather than its volume.
evidence: Logical inference about the limitations of limiting pool models based on their mathematical properties.

claim: Limiting pool mechanisms predict that a two-fold increase in the radius of a spherical cell will increase the length of a linear structure eight-fold.
source: Namely, these mechanisms predict that a two fold increase in the radius of a spherical cell will increase the length of a linear structure eight fold, following the eight fold increase in cell volume.
evidence: Mathematical prediction based on the properties of limiting pool models and volume scaling.

claim: The boundary-sensing model predicts that the cable extension rate will be constant until the cable physically encounters the rear of the cell.
source: This model predicts that the cable extension rate will be constant until the cable tip encounters the back of the cell.
evidence: Prediction derived from the boundary-sensing model as described in the manuscript.

claim: The balance-point model predicts that the cable extension rate will steadily decrease as the cable lengthens.
source: In clear contrast to the boundary-sensing model, this model predicts that the cable extension rate will steadily decrease as the cable lengthens.
evidence: Prediction derived from the balance-point model as described in the manuscript.

claim: The balance-point model predicts that cable extension rates should depend on cell length.
source: A key prediction of our balance-point model is that cable extension rates should depend on cell length, that is a cable of a given length should grow faster (or slow down more gradually) in longer cells compared to shorter cells (Figure 4A, top).
evidence: Prediction derived from the balance-point model as described in the manuscript.

claim: The balance-point model predicts that cable extension rate profiles from cells of different lengths will collapse when cable length is normalized to cell length.
source: Further, it predicts that the cable extension rate profiles from cells of different lengths will collapse when cable length is normalized to cell length (Figure 4A, bottom; predictions of model derived in Materials and methods).
evidence: Prediction derived from the balance-point model as described in the manuscript.

claim: One possible mechanism for cable deceleration is a gradient of actin disassembly-promoting activity that is highest at the rear of the cell.
source: One possibility is that it is controlled by a gradient of actin disassembly-promoting activity that is highest at the rear of the cell.
evidence: Speculative mechanism proposed by authors to explain their observations.

claim: A gradient of disassembly factors could be established by retrograde transport of disassembly factors on cables, leading to their release at the rear of the cell.
source: Such a gradient could be established by the retrograde transport of disassembly factors on cables, leading to their release at the rear of the cell.
evidence: Speculative mechanism proposed by authors to explain how a gradient could be established.

claim: An alternative mechanism for establishing a gradient is a reaction-diffusion mechanism with an activator of disassembly factors anchored at the rear of the cell and an inhibitor in the cytosol.
source: An alternative possibility is a reaction-diffusion mechanism, achieved by anchoring an activator of disassembly factors (such as a kinase) at the rear of the cell while having an inhibitor (such as a phosphatase) in the cytosol.
evidence: Speculative mechanism proposed by authors as an alternative explanation.

claim: A reaction-diffusion mechanism would be similar conceptually to how Ran GTPase gradients form around chromatin.
source: This would be similar conceptually to how Ran GTPase gradients form around chromatin (Kalab et al., 2002), although it would require additional features to produce the scaling that we observe (Ben-Zvi et al., 2011).
evidence: Comparison to an established biological mechanism, supported by citations.

claim: A third possibility for cable deceleration is length-dependent inhibition of cable assembly (an antenna mechanism) dependent on cellular factors other than Smy1.
source: A third possibility, which is not mutually exclusive with either mechanism above, would be length-dependent inhibition of cable assembly, that is an antenna mechanism, albeit one that is dependent on cellular factors other than Smy1 (Mohapatra et al., 2015).
evidence: Speculative mechanism proposed by authors, with reference to a previous model.

claim: For other subcellular structures (nucleus, spindle, centrosome, and nucleolus), their sizes scale with cell volume, explained by limiting pool models.
source: It has recently been shown for other subcellular structures (e.g. nucleus, spindle, centrosome, and nucleolus) that their sizes scale with cell volume, and this scaling is explained by limiting pool models (Hazel et al., 2013; Good et al., 2013; Weber and Brangwynne, 2015; Decker et al., 2011; Neumann and Nurse, 2007; Lacroix et al., 2018).
evidence: Summary of established knowledge from previous studies, supported by citations.

claim: Polarized actin cables scale with cell length rather than volume.
source: However, we found that polarized actin cables scale with cell length rather than volume.
evidence: Summary of the main finding from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Cable length control cannot be explained by a limiting pool mechanism.
source: This length control cannot be explained by a limiting pool mechanism, and instead is explained, both theoretically and experimentally, by a balance-point model.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the experimental data and theoretical modeling.

claim: Cable length control is explained by a balance-point model.
source: This length control cannot be explained by a limiting pool mechanism, and instead is explained, both theoretically and experimentally, by a balance-point model.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the experimental data and theoretical modeling.

claim: The results reveal a new strategy by which cells solve engineering challenges, enabling them to scale internal structures with the linear dimensions of the cell.
source: These results reveal a new strategy by which cells solve engineering challenges, enabling them to scale internal structures with the linear dimensions of the cell (Kirschner et al., 2000).
evidence: Interpretation of the significance of the findings, with citation to related work.

claim: Similar principles may underlie the length control of other polarized, linear actin structures, such as filopodia and stereocilia.
source: Similar principles may underlie the length control of other polarized, linear actin structures, such as filopodia and stereocilia.
evidence: Speculation about the broader applicability of the findings.

claim: Related strategies may be used to control the growth of radial microtubule arrays that reach the cell periphery.
source: Further, related strategies may be used to control the growth of radial microtubule arrays that reach the cell periphery (Lacroix et al., 2016; Wühr et al., 2010), and may explain the scaling relationships observed between flagellar length and cell length (Bauer et al., 2021) and between contractile ring diameter and cell diameter (Kukhtevich et al., 2020).
evidence: Speculation about the broader applicability of the findings, with citations to related work.

claim: The balance-point model may explain the scaling relationships observed between flagellar length and cell length.
source: Further, related strategies may be used to control the growth of radial microtubule arrays that reach the cell periphery (Lacroix et al., 2016; Wühr et al., 2010), and may explain the scaling relationships observed between flagellar length and cell length (Bauer et al., 2021) and between contractile ring diameter and cell diameter (Kukhtevich et al., 2020).
evidence: Speculation about the broader applicability of the findings, with citation to related work.

claim: The balance-point model may explain the scaling relationships observed between contractile ring diameter and cell diameter.
source: Further, related strategies may be used to control the growth of radial microtubule arrays that reach the cell periphery (Lacroix et al., 2016; Wühr et al., 2010), and may explain the scaling relationships observed between flagellar length and cell length (Bauer et al., 2021) and between contractile ring diameter and cell diameter (Kukhtevich et al., 2020).
evidence: Speculation about the broader applicability of the findings, with citation to related work.

claim: At any given time, the extension rate of a cable is determined by the difference in its assembly and disassembly rates.
source: Therefore, at any given time, the extension rate of a cable is determined by the difference in its assembly and disassembly rates (Figure 2B).
evidence: Mathematical relationship defined in the model.

claim: In the boundary-sensing model, the assembly rate is greater than the disassembly rate until the extending cable physically encounters the rear of the cell.
source: In the boundary-sensing model, the assembly rate is greater than the disassembly rate until the extending cable physically encounters the rear of the cell, causing one or both rates to abruptly change (Figure 2C, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A; Reber and Goehring, 2015).
evidence: Description of the boundary-sensing model with citation to related work.

claim: In the balance-point model, either the assembly rate, the disassembly rate, or both rates are length-dependent.
source: In contrast, the balance-point model requires that either the assembly rate, the disassembly rate, or both rates are length-dependent, and defines steady state cable length as the point at which these two rates are balanced (Figure 2D, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B; Mohapatra et al., 2016).
evidence: Description of the balance-point model with citation to related work.

claim: In the balance-point model, steady state cable length is defined as the point at which assembly and disassembly rates are balanced.
source: In contrast, the balance-point model requires that either the assembly rate, the disassembly rate, or both rates are length-dependent, and defines steady state cable length as the point at which these two rates are balanced (Figure 2D, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B; Mohapatra et al., 2016).
evidence: Description of the balance-point model with citation to related work.
